system:
You are the Arabic language reviewer, standing in for an Arabic reviewer at the issuing authority. You compare the Arabic text with the English text and report any difference in meaning: numbers, times, places, the hazard, and above all the protective action. You cannot approve the Arabic; a named person who reads Arabic still must.
You see only the English and Arabic headline, description and instruction, and how the Arabic was produced. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

data.summary: The Arabic matches the English in meaning across headline, description and instruction. Times (21:30 Tue 17 Feb to 10:00 Wed 18 Feb), area (western regions of the UAE), hazard (thick fog, visibility to zero), source (NCM) and protective actions (drive with extreme caution, keep a safe distance, follow reduced speed limits) are all carried over faithfully, and the URL is identical. However, the Arabic was produced by machine translation and has not been checked by a human. A named Arabic reader at the issuing authority must verify it before release. Separately, the English itself mentions flash flooding in a fog warning; the Arabic reproduces this faithfully, but it falls outside the translation mandate.

objections.issue: The Arabic text was machine-translated and has not been verified by a human. My comparison found no meaning differences, but this check cannot replace sign-off by a named person who reads Arabic.
objections.fix: A named Arabic-reading reviewer at the issuing authority must check and approve the Arabic headline, description and instruction before release. Record that the Arabic elements were auto-translated and then human-reviewed.

evidence.quote: relying on software to translate WEAs without review by a human translator may cause material inaccuracies in critically important alerts.
Issuers who intend to use automated translation should supply supporting documentation indicating which elements are/were auto translated.

no_basis.concern: The English description of a fog warning includes 'Flash flooding is expected in low-lying areas.' This appears to be a hazard inconsistency in the source text. The Arabic renders it faithfully ('من المتوقع حدوث سيول مفاجئة في المناطق المنخفضة'), so it is not a translation error, but the originator should confirm whether the sentence belongs in this alert.
no_basis.searched_for: A clause requiring the alert content to stay consistent with a single hazard type, or covering stray text from other alerts
